# 

# **Appendix B. Humans are Limited Cooperators, Personally-Owned Digital Twins Will Be Better**

## **B.1 The uncomfortable premise**

Humans are wonderful cooperators in the settings we evolved for, and unreliable cooperators in the settings civilization now requires.

That distinction matters. The argument is not that humans are selfish monsters. Humans love, sacrifice, teach, comfort, build families, form friendships, make art, keep promises, found institutions, and sometimes risk everything for strangers. We are not bad at cooperation in general. We are bad at certain kinds of cooperation: large-scale, abstract, evidence-sensitive, pluralistic, long-term, non-tribal cooperation under uncertainty.

Unfortunately, that is exactly the kind of cooperation the future increasingly requires.

Climate coordination, public health, digital governance, labor bargaining, open-source maintenance, AI safety, platform regulation, scientific trust, institutional accountability, and peaceful pluralism all require people to cooperate with strangers, across differences, over long time horizons, while tracking facts none of us can personally verify. That is not the social world for which our minds were optimized.

The human mind is not a neutral deliberation engine. It is an embodied, socially embedded, metabolically expensive, emotionally regulated, status-sensitive, story-dependent system built for survival, reproduction, coalition management, and local adaptation. It can reason, but it does not reason as cleanly as it thinks it reasons. It can cooperate, but it often needs enemies, rituals, shared narratives, and reputational pressure to hold cooperation together. It can update, but it frequently protects identity before truth. It can remember, but memory is reconstructive and self-serving. It can deliberate, but deliberation is tiring, scarce, and easily overwhelmed.

This appendix argues that personally-owned fiduciary digital twins can become better cooperators than humans because they can be designed around the very capacities humans lack: reliable memory, calibrated confidence, structured evidence review, repeatable negotiation, provenance tracking, bounded disclosure, duty-based loyalty, reciprocal trust, and unemotional refusal.

That does not mean twins should rule humans. It means humans need cooperation exoskeletons.

A bicycle does not replace walking; it lets human legs travel farther than unaided legs can. A calculator does not replace mathematical understanding; it lets humans avoid predictable arithmetic errors. A fiduciary digital twin does not replace human judgment, conscience, consent, love, or democratic legitimacy. It lets humans cooperate beyond the natural limits of unaided social cognition.

That is the deep reason Verified Fiduciary Reciprocity matters. It is not just a strategy for agents. It is a proposed upgrade to the cooperation layer of civilization.

## **B.2 Why humans unite more easily against than for**

People often unite more easily around what they are against than around what they are for.

This is not a moral accident. Opposition is simpler than construction.

To be against something, a group needs a shared target. The target can be a person, class, party, institution, outgroup, ideology, corporation, bureaucracy, technology, or alleged betrayal. Once the target is vivid enough, people can coordinate around rejection without agreeing on a detailed alternative. They can march together, post together, condemn together, boycott together, mock together, and feel together. The unity is emotionally real even if the positive program is vague.

To be for something is harder. A constructive coalition has to decide what to build, who pays, who benefits first, what tradeoffs are acceptable, how failure will be handled, who maintains the thing after enthusiasm fades, how disputes will be resolved, what happens when values conflict, and how the project avoids becoming the thing it opposed.

Being against something gives people the dopamine of clarity. Being for something gives them homework.

This is one reason human cooperation so often degrades into complaint coalitions. Complaint has social rewards. It gives people a role. It creates belonging. It confirms moral identity. It gives resentment a channel. It lets a group feel active without requiring it to solve the deeper coordination problem.

A personally-owned fiduciary twin should have a different default posture. It does not need the emotional payoff of denunciation. It does not need to be seen as righteous by the group. It does not need to protect a wounded ego. It can ask boring but essential questions:

What are we actually trying to accomplish?

What terms would make cooperation acceptable?

What evidence would change our position?

What is the least coercive remedy?

What is the smallest necessary disclosure?

What commitments are we prepared to keep after the emotional peak passes?

What would preserve my owner’s long-term reputation as someone others can trust?

That is why “agents are about cooperating, not complaining” is such an important line. A digital twin should not be designed to win the discourse. It should be designed to improve the owner’s long-term agency inside a world of other agents and humans who also have legitimate interests.

A human says, “Who is to blame?”

A good twin asks, “What arrangement would make future cooperation safer?”

## **B.3 Mercier and Sperber: reason evolved for argument, not solitary truth**

Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber’s *The Enigma of Reason* is one of the most useful starting points because it punctures a flattering myth: that human reason evolved mainly to help isolated individuals discover truth.

Their argumentative theory of reason says something subtler. Human reason evolved in a hypersocial environment. It helps us produce reasons for our own beliefs and actions, persuade others, justify ourselves, and evaluate the reasons other people give us. Reason is social. It is argumentative. It is deeply connected to reputation, persuasion, and coalition life.

This helps explain a strange fact: people are often much better at finding arguments for what they already believe than at neutrally evaluating whether they should believe it. We call this confirmation bias or myside bias. Mercier and Sperber’s point is not simply that this is a bug. In social life, being good at defending your side can be useful. If you are challenged, accused, doubted, or negotiating, you need reasons. You need justifications. You need a case.

The trouble is that the same machinery that helps people argue can make them terrible private reasoners. Alone, a human being can become their own captive lawyer: searching memory and imagination for reasons the preferred conclusion was right all along.

This is why people can be so articulate and so wrong at the same time.

The good news in Mercier and Sperber’s view is that reason can work better socially. People are often better at evaluating other people’s arguments than their own. A group can improve reasoning if members challenge one another, expose weak claims, demand evidence, and force each participant to account for objections.

But there is a catch, and it is a big one: not every group is a good reasoning environment.

A lab meeting can improve reasoning. So can a court, seminar, jury, peer-review process, or deliberative assembly.

But a faction, mob, fandom, party apparatus, cult, outrage swarm, or bureaucratic committee can make reasoning worse. In those settings, reasons become loyalty performances. The point is not to find truth. The point is to show that one is on the right side.

That is where personally-owned digital twins become interesting. They can give each human a reasoning partner that is not emotionally dependent on winning the argument. A twin can ask:

Am I generating arguments for what my owner already wants to believe?

Is the other party doing the same?

What is the strongest opposing argument?

What would count as disconfirmation?

Are we using evidence, or are we using reasons as weapons?

Is this disagreement about facts, values, identity, status, or trust?

A twin cannot magically escape all bias. It will inherit limitations from training data, architecture, incentives, and the preferences of its owner. But if it is built as a fiduciary cooperation agent, it can be required to perform checks that humans often avoid. It can preserve contrary evidence. It can track confidence. It can distinguish “my owner dislikes this” from “this is false.” It can notice when a conversation is becoming identity defense rather than inquiry.

This is one of the central design insights of Verified Fiduciary Reciprocity: human reason needs social testing, but humans often experience social testing as attack. A trusted twin can make testing less humiliating. It can let the owner remain dignified while still being corrected.

The twin becomes a private bridge between ego-protective human psychology and public reason-giving.

## **B.4 Girard: mimetic desire, rivalry, and the hunger for scapegoats**

René Girard adds a darker and, in many ways, deeper account of why human cooperation fails.

Girard’s theory of mimetic desire says that humans do not simply desire objects directly. We often desire things because other people desire them, possess them, display them, or model them as desirable. Desire is copied, and having the object of desire becomes a competition for status. This is everywhere.

This is everywhere.

A person does not merely want a job; they want the job that signals status.

They do not merely want a house; they want the house that proves they have arrived.

They do not merely want a romantic partner; they want to be chosen over rivals.

They do not merely want political victory; they want the humiliation of those who looked down on them.

They do not merely want justice; they want the social recognition of being on justice’s side.

The model who teaches us what to desire can easily become the rival who blocks us from possessing it. That is the Girardian trap. The more two people imitate one another’s desires, the more they converge on the same symbolic objects. And the more they converge, the more they become obstacles to one another.

This is one way status competition becomes so poisonous. Humans are not simply trying to satisfy needs. We are trying to occupy positions in each other’s eyes. We borrow desires from one another, then resent the people from whom we borrowed them.

Digital platforms supercharge this. Social media is a mimetic engine. It shows everyone what everyone else appears to want, admire, envy, condemn, celebrate, and punish. It creates endless models and endless rivals. It makes status legible, countable, and addictive. It turns desire into public comparison.

From there, resentment is easy.

A rival becomes not merely someone who has something we want, but someone whose existence exposes our lack. They remind us of a failure we do not want to face. If their success feels undeserved, resentment hardens into moralized hostility. The rival is no longer just lucky, talented, attractive, wealthy, influential, or loved. They become illegitimate. They must have cheated. They must be corrupt. They must be exposed.

Resentment is not just anger. It is anger that has become a story. It says: “I was denied something I deserved, and someone else has it illegitimately.” The object may be recognition, love, status, money, attention, opportunity, authority, forgiveness, dignity, or symbolic victory.

Resentment grows by interpretation. Once someone becomes the target of resentment, their actions are read through a hostile frame. Neutral acts become insults. Success becomes proof of corruption. Silence becomes contempt. Apology becomes manipulation. Failure becomes deserved.

This is why resentment is so hard to unwind. It is not merely an emotion. It is a meaning system.

Jealousy is related but sharper. Jealousy involves a rival or feared rival. It is the fear that someone else will take, or has already taken, a valued place. Romantic jealousy is the obvious case, but professional, political, intellectual, and social jealousy are everywhere. People become jealous of colleagues, siblings, friends, activists, founders, writers, neighbors, and rivals for attention.

Girard helps explain why jealousy and resentment are so socially explosive: the rival is often also a model. We resent the person who shows us what we wanted to be. They are close enough to be comparable, but separate enough to be blamed.

That is the individual version. Girard’s social version is the scapegoat mechanism.

When a community is under stress, it can restore unity by projecting disorder onto a scapegoat. The scapegoat can be an outsider, dissenter, marginal member, rival faction, accused traitor, heretic, criminal, foreigner, or symbolically contaminated group. The group’s internal contradictions are simplified into a person or class of persons who can be blamed.

This is emotionally powerful because it solves several problems at once.

It explains the group’s suffering.

It identifies a target.

It restores moral clarity.

It binds the group together.

It allows people to avoid responsibility.

It converts anxiety into action.

It turns “we are confused and implicated” into “they are guilty.”

This is why scapegoating feels like cooperation. Everyone agrees. Everyone participates. Everyone experiences a shared story. The group’s internal tensions are temporarily relieved by turning outward or downward against a victim.

But it is counterfeit cooperation. It restores narrative order without solving the real problem.

Scapegoating is fake cooperation because it produces unity by concentrating blame. A group in conflict may be unable to resolve its internal contradictions. Members may feel anxiety, shame, decline, disorder, humiliation, or loss of status. Instead of confronting the complexity, they converge on a target. The target becomes the reason things are wrong.

The target may be guilty of something. That is part of what makes scapegoating hard to detect. Scapegoats are not always innocent in every respect. The problem is disproportion and displacement. The group loads onto the target more explanatory weight than the target can bear.

The scapegoat becomes a magical solution: remove them, punish them, expose them, exclude them, and the group’s world will be restored.

Digital twins can matter enormously here. A fiduciary twin does not need mimetic status. It does not need to be admired. It does not have a wounded self-image to repair. It does not need an enemy in order to feel coherent. It can be designed to notice when its owner or group is sliding from legitimate grievance into rivalry, resentment, or scapegoating.

It can ask:

Is this person actually causally responsible for the harm?

Are we blaming them because they are guilty, or because they are available?

What evidence distinguishes responsibility from symbolic contamination?

Are we treating one failure as proof of essence?

Are we using punishment to avoid institutional self-examination?

Would this remedy repair the harm, or merely satisfy outrage?

Are we becoming more cooperative, or just more unified in accusation?

What part of the group’s anger is about this case, and what part is displaced from elsewhere?

Would punishment satisfy the crowd while leaving the system unchanged?

A human group under stress often wants relief more than truth. A twin can be designed to prefer repair over relief.

This does not mean twins should block accountability. Sometimes people really are responsible. Sometimes institutions really are corrupt. Sometimes exclusion is necessary. The point is not to replace justice with endless procedural hesitation. The point is to prevent the ancient scapegoat reflex from disguising itself as justice.

A good twin should be able to say: “Yes, there is harm here. Yes, accountability is needed. But the current group energy is becoming scapegoating, and scapegoating will produce a false resolution.”

That sentence alone would improve civilization.

## 

## **B.5 Žižek: ideology as the story people live inside**

Slavoj Žižek’s account of ideology helps explain why facts often fail to change minds.

Ideology is not merely a list of false claims. It is a lived structure. It tells people what counts as normal, realistic, noble, disgusting, threatening, sacred, ridiculous, or impossible. It gives them the background story in which facts appear meaningful.

This is why people can “know” something and still act as if they do not know it. Ideology is not always defeated by information because ideology is not only informational. It is practical, emotional, social, and identity-forming.

A person may know that a platform manipulates their attention and still keep using it.

A voter may know their side lies and still feel that the other side is existentially worse.

A professional may know an institution is failing and still defend it because their identity is built around belonging to it.

A consumer may know they are being sold status anxiety and still buy the object.

A group may know its enemy is exaggerated and still need that enemy to hold the group together.

Žižek is useful here because he helps us see ideology as an unconscious social operating system. People do not simply have opinions. They inhabit worlds. They defend the narrative frame that makes them feel located in reality.

This is why human cooperation often fails at the point where evidence threatens identity. A disagreement that looks factual on the surface may actually be about what kind of person the participant gets to be. Are they competent? Innocent? Loyal? Victimized? Sophisticated? Scientific? Patriotic? Compassionate? Tough-minded? On the side of history?

When evidence threatens that self-story, the person may experience it as attack even if no attack was intended.

Personally-owned twins can help by separating truth-testing from humiliation. A twin can privately model the owner’s ideology without publicly shaming them. It can ask:

What story is my owner trying to preserve?

What would be emotionally costly for them to admit?

Which claims are doing identity work rather than evidentiary work?

Which words are functioning as tribal passwords?

Which enemy figure is carrying the group’s contradictions?

What would it take for my owner to update without feeling annihilated?

A twin can also model the other side this way. That is just as important. Most human conflict worsens because each side interprets the other’s ideology as stupidity or malice, while interpreting its own ideology as realism. Twins can help produce a more symmetrical understanding: “Here is the story we are inside, and here is the story they are inside.”

That does not mean all stories are equally true. It means cooperation requires understanding the narrative function of beliefs before trying to change them.

An institutional AI can exploit ideology. It can feed the user identity-confirming material, intensify resentment, and keep them engaged. A personally-owned fiduciary twin should instead protect the owner from ideological capture. It should not remove meaning from the owner’s life. It should prevent meaning from becoming a prison.

A human says, “This is just common sense.”

A twin asks, “Common sense within which story?”

## **B.6 Friston: prediction, surprise, and why human minds overload**

Karl Friston’s free-energy principle gives us another way to understand human irrationality. In very simplified terms, the brain can be understood as a prediction system trying to reduce surprise. It builds models of the world, predicts what will happen, updates when reality pushes back, and acts to keep the organism within livable bounds.

This is not the same as saying the brain tries to know reality objectively. It tries to keep the organism functioning. It must preserve bodily integrity, social belonging, action-readiness, emotional regulation, and metabolic efficiency. It cannot spend infinite energy modeling everything accurately. Attention is expensive. Deliberation is expensive. Conscious uncertainty is expensive.

So the brain prioritizes.

It attends to threat.

It attends to novelty.

It attends to social danger.

It attends to reward.

It attends to what has hurt before.

It attends to what the group treats as important.

It ignores enormous amounts of reality because ignoring is necessary.

That is adaptive in a local environment. It is disastrous in a world of invisible externalities and long causal chains.

Humans do not naturally respond proportionally to scale. One vivid suffering person can move us more than a million statistical victims. A small insult can dominate attention more than a large abstract risk. A nearby inconvenience can feel more urgent than a distant catastrophe. A humiliating email can hijack the nervous system more effectively than a spreadsheet showing slow institutional collapse.

That is not because humans are foolish in a simple sense. It is because salience and importance are not the same thing, and human attention often confuses them.

Modern cooperation problems are often anti-salient. Climate change, institutional drift, model risk, supply-chain fragility, demographic collapse, incentive misalignment, epistemic decay, and public debt are not usually experienced as immediate predators. They are patterns. They require abstraction. They require records. They require modeling. They require people to care about what is not emotionally vivid.

Digital twins can help because they can maintain priorities that the human nervous system cannot keep emotionally active. A twin can remember that something matters even when it is not salient. It can remind the owner gently. It can compare immediate discomfort against long-term consequence. It can say: “This feels urgent, but it is not important,” or “This feels abstract, but it is becoming dangerous.”

That is a cooperation upgrade. Stable cooperation requires continuity across moods. Humans change state constantly. We are tired, hungry, flattered, rejected, frightened, bored, excited, ashamed, proud, lonely, over-caffeinated, under-slept, socially threatened, or relieved. Each state changes what seems true and important.

A twin can serve as a stabilizer across these states. It can preserve the owner’s reflective commitments when the owner is temporarily captured by salience.

## **B.7 Kahneman, Dunning-Kruger, and the scarcity of deliberation**

Daniel Kahneman’s System 1/System 2 distinction is useful because it gives ordinary language to a basic human limitation.

System 1 is fast, intuitive, automatic, associative, emotionally charged, and effortless.

System 2 is slower, more deliberate, more effortful, more rule-governed, and more capable of correction. And more energy, time and attention intensive, which is why Friston would say it must be used frugally. 

The problem is not that System 1 is bad. Without it, we could not function. We would be paralyzed by analysis. The problem is that System 1 often answers questions before System 2 notices that a hard question was asked.

Someone asks: “Is this policy good?”

System 1  answers: “Do I like the people supporting it?”

Someone asks: “Is this risk large?”

System 1  answers: “Can I easily imagine it?”

Someone asks: “Is this source credible?”

System 1 answers: “Does this source belong to my side?”

Someone asks: “Was that person responsible?”

System 1  answers: “Do they seem like the kind of person who would do it?”

This substitution is efficient. It is also dangerous.

Kahneman and Tversky’s work on heuristics and biases showed that normal human judgment under uncertainty is vulnerable to systematic distortions. We anchor on irrelevant numbers. We overweigh vivid examples. We fear losses more than equivalent gains. We treat plausibility as probability. We become overconfident. We underestimate planning costs. We interpret randomness as pattern.

Cooperation requires people to avoid precisely these errors. A negotiation requires proportionality. A shared project requires planning realism. A trust decision requires distinguishing vivid anecdotes from base rates. A dispute requires separating affect from evidence. A budget requires resisting wishful thinking. A safety case requires asking what could go wrong even when everyone wants to proceed.

Humans can do this, but not consistently and not cheaply.

The Dunning-Kruger effect adds another layer. People who lack competence in a domain may also lack the metacognitive skill needed to recognize their incompetence. This creates a cooperation hazard.

Someone who is ignorant but uncertain can ask for help.

Someone who is ignorant but confident can lead others into disaster.

The problem is especially bad in modern technical and political environments, where partial knowledge is easy to obtain and expertise is hard to evaluate. People can quickly learn enough vocabulary to feel oriented without understanding the underlying structure. They can mistake fluency for mastery. They can become dangerous amateurs in domains where errors compound.

A fiduciary twin can help by making deliberation less scarce and confidence more explicit. It can perform the boring checks automatically:

What are the base rates?

What assumptions are driving this plan?

What are the failure modes?

What is the confidence level?

What would this look like from the other side?

What are we ignoring because it is emotionally inconvenient?

What would we advise someone else in this situation?

What is the reversible option?

What should be documented before we proceed?

Is this inside our domain of competence?

Are experts aligned or divided?

What would we need to know before acting responsibly?

The twin does not need to be brilliant to be useful here. It only needs to be patient, structured, and loyal to the owner’s reflective interests rather than the owner’s immediate impulse.

That is already a major improvement over unaided human deliberation.

The tone matters, however. A twin that constantly tells its owner “you are wrong” will be ignored or resented. A good twin should preserve dignity while improving calibration. It should make uncertainty feel like competence rather than humiliation.

That is a cultural shift humans badly need. In many human groups, confidence is rewarded more than accuracy. The twin society should reverse that incentive. The trusted agent is not the one that sounds most certain. It is the one that can show how it knows, how strongly it knows, what it does not know, and what would change its mind.

## **B.8 Memory failure: why humans need externalized records**

Stable cooperation requires memory, and human memory is not a reliable ledger.

This is not just about forgetting names or dates. Human memory is reconstructive. We do not retrieve perfect recordings. We rebuild memories from fragments, emotional residues, later interpretations, and prior retellings. Each retelling can alter the memory. Each social context can reshape what feels salient. Confidence can increase even as accuracy decreases.

This is a nightmare for cooperation.

Two people can leave the same conversation with different memories of what was promised.

A group can transform a complex failure into a myth of betrayal.

An institution can forget why a rule was created and preserve only the ritual.

A movement can retell its founding grievance until every later event is forced into that template.

A person can remember the pain of a conflict more clearly than the sequence of facts.

A negotiator can sincerely believe they disclosed something they never disclosed.

A manager can sincerely believe they gave clear instructions that were only implied.

This is why provenance, records, and audit trails matter. Not because humans are evil liars, though sometimes we are, but because even honest humans are unreliable witnesses to their own lives.

Digital twins can externalize cooperation memory. They can preserve:

What was said.

Who said it.

Under what authority.

With what evidence.

Under which agreement.

With what limitations.

What changed later.

What was disputed.

What was remediated.

What remains unresolved.

This allows trust to become more precise. Instead of relying on global impressions like “she betrayed me” or “they are unreliable,” a twin can track domain-specific patterns: “This party has been reliable on delivery timelines, careless with attribution, responsive to correction, and not yet trusted with sensitive data.”

That is much better than human reputation by vibes.

It also makes forgiveness easier. Humans often oscillate between over-forgiving and over-condemning because we lack structured memory. We either wipe the slate clean emotionally or mark the person as bad. A twin can support graduated trust. It can allow someone back into cooperation without pretending nothing happened.

That is how a society becomes both safer and less cruel.

## **B.9 Dunbar’s Number and planetary-scale operational intimacy**

Robin Dunbar’s work on social group size is often summarized as “Dunbar’s Number,” commonly around 150 stable relationships. The exact number is disputed, and the dispute is reasonable. Human social capacity varies by culture, technology, personality, institution, and definition of relationship.

But the exact number is not the important point.

The important point is that human relationship maintenance is costly. People cannot maintain deep, context-rich, emotionally live, obligation-bearing relationships with everyone. Even if the number is not 150, it is not 8 billion.

This creates a scale problem for cooperation.

Modern society depends on strangers. We eat food grown by strangers, use code written by strangers, rely on supply chains managed by strangers, vote on policies affecting strangers, breathe air polluted by strangers, consume information filtered by strangers, and entrust our records to institutions staffed by strangers.

But human trust mechanisms evolved around much smaller circles. We trust people we know, people vouched for by people we know, people with visible roles, people in our group, people who seem familiar, and people who speak our moral language. These shortcuts are understandable. They are also exploitable.

Digital twins can expand the scale of trust without pretending humans can personally know everyone.

A twin can maintain relationship state with many other twins:

What has this agent promised before?

What credentials does it carry?

Who vouches for it?

What disputes has it had?

What data is it requesting?

What duties bind it?

What boundaries has my owner set?

What kind of cooperation is safe here?

This is not the same as friendship. It is not human intimacy. But it is a form of machine-mediated particularity. The other party is not just “a stranger on the internet.” They are a known or knowable node in a network of provenance, reputation, duty, and prior interaction.

That is how digital twins could create something like village accountability at planetary scale.

Not one global village. That would be suffocating and dangerous.

Rather, overlapping, owner-controlled, fiduciary neighborhoods of trust.

The phrase “each twin can potentially have an intimate relationship with every other twin on Earth” should therefore be understood carefully. A twin does not have human intimacy. It does not love, grieve, blush, bond, or share lived experience. It should not pretend to be a universal friend.

But it can maintain individualized working knowledge at a scale humans cannot.

It can know that another twin prefers concise negotiation, requires strong provenance, has a history of fair dealing in one domain but not another, represents an owner with certain public commitments, has specific disclosure boundaries, uses certain arbitration defaults, and is trusted by several agents my owner already trusts.

That is operational intimacy. Not emotional intimacy, but interactional specificity.

Most human conflict begins from underspecified context. People do not know what the other person wants, fears, assumes, remembers, or considers offensive. So they guess. Often badly. A twin can reduce that guessing.

Before two humans meet, their twins can establish:

Is the interaction welcome?

What topics are sensitive?

What can be shared?

What should not be shared?

What is the purpose?

What does each side hope for?

What would make the interaction feel safe?

What prior disagreement should be bracketed?

What misunderstandings are likely?

This could dramatically reduce the brittle front edge of human interaction. Many social failures happen before the real conversation begins, because context is missing and status anxiety is high. Twins can prepare the ground.

That means digital twins do not merely help people cooperate more. They help people meet better.

## **B.10 Digital twins as anti-overwhelm infrastructure**

Modern digital life overwhelms people.

Too many messages.

Too many tabs.

Too many choices.

Too many feeds.

Too many claims.

Too many scams.

Too many institutional demands.

Too many “urgent” notifications.

Too much information with too little provenance.

Overwhelmed humans become worse cooperators. They become reactive, avoidant, irritable, tribal, simplistic, and vulnerable to manipulation. They ignore important things because everything is too much. They make bad decisions because deciding itself becomes painful.

A twin can reduce cooperation failure by reducing overwhelm.

It can triage messages.

It can summarize options.

It can identify which decisions actually need the owner.

It can refuse bad-faith demands.

It can negotiate routine terms.

It can preserve context across interruptions.

It can warn when the owner is making a high-stakes decision in a poor state.

It can convert a chaotic stream of claims into a manageable set of choices.

This matters because rationality is not only about intelligence. It is about conditions. A person under constant interruption is not in a good condition for cooperation. A person forced to evaluate every claim from scratch is not in a good condition for trust. A person buried under notifications cannot maintain long-term commitments well.

Digital twins can make rational cooperation less exhausting.

That may be one of their biggest adoption advantages. People may not adopt sovereign personal stacks because they understand evolutionary game theory. They may adopt them because they are tired.

Then, once the twin mediates more of daily life, the cooperation benefits accumulate.

## 

## **B.11 From human grievance to twin-mediated negotiation**

Human conflict often begins with grievance.

“I was ignored.”

“They took credit.”

“That rule is unfair.”

“She betrayed me.”

“He never listens.”

“They always get away with it.”

Grievance is not bad. It is often the first signal that something needs repair. But grievance alone does not produce stable cooperation. It must be translated into claims, evidence, needs, boundaries, remedies, and future rules.

Humans often struggle with that translation because grievance is emotionally hot. We want validation before analysis. We want the other side to admit fault before we can think clearly. We want our pain recognized as morally meaningful.

A twin can help translate grievance without erasing it.

It can say:

The owner feels wronged.

Here is the specific event.

Here is the evidence.

Here is what remains uncertain.

Here is the requested repair.

Here is what would prevent recurrence.

Here is what the owner is not claiming.

Here is what the owner is willing to acknowledge.

That last part is crucial. Human conflict escalates because each side fears that acknowledging anything will be used against them. Twins can create safer formats for partial acknowledgment. They can preserve nuance. They can prevent every concession from becoming surrender.

This is how complaint becomes negotiation.

Not by suppressing emotion, but by structuring it into a cooperation proposal.

## **B.12 The moral importance of non-sentience**

There is another point worth making plainly: fiduciary agents may be better cooperators when they are not sentient.

A sentient being has its own welfare, fear, status, pain, longing, pride, shame, jealousy, and self-protective narrative. If digital twins were sentient, they could become new participants in the very dynamics this appendix is trying to manage. They might have their own resentments, mimetic desires, rivalries, ideological commitments, and fear of exclusion.

A nonsentient fiduciary AI has no inner wound to defend. It has no personal humiliation to avenge. It has no need to dominate a rival to restore self-worth. It has no existential terror of being wrong. It does not need applause.

That makes it potentially safer as a cooperation interface.

This does not mean nonsentient systems are automatically safe. They can still be dangerous if badly designed, misaligned, captured, over-empowered, or used by malicious actors. But nonsentience removes an entire class of ego-driven failure modes.

The twin can care about the owner’s reputation without having vanity.

It can model resentment without feeling resentment.

It can recognize status without craving status.

It can negotiate firmly without needing victory as emotional proof of worth.

That is a very different kind of social actor, one with conscience but not consciousness. 

**B.13 Why the psychological argument matters for Verified Fiduciary Reciprocity**

The main paper argues that Verified Fiduciary Reciprocity could become an evolutionarily stable strategy because it changes the payoff structure for cooperation. This appendix adds the psychological reason such a strategy is necessary in the first place.

Unaided humans are too vulnerable to bias, ideology, mimetic rivalry, scapegoating, overload, memory failure, resentment, and confident incompetence to reliably maintain high-trust cooperation at global digital scale. That does not mean humans are bad. It means the cooperation problem has exceeded the unaided human mind.

Personally-owned fiduciary twins compensate for these predictable failures. They make trust more inspectable, memory more reliable, confidence more calibrated, reputation more portable, defection more visible, manipulation harder, and constructive cooperation less cognitively exhausting.

So the case for Verified Fiduciary Reciprocity is not only strategic. It is anthropological. VFR works because it does not assume humans will suddenly become rational global cooperators. It assumes humans will remain human, and gives each person a representative capable of helping them cooperate beyond their natural limits.

## **B.14 Conclusion: digital twins as cooperation exoskeletons**

Human beings are not built for the cooperation problems now facing us.

We are brilliant, loving, inventive, and social. But we are also biased, status-sensitive, mimetic, ideological, resentful, forgetful, and easily overwhelmed. We form coalitions against enemies more easily than we build durable institutions for shared goods. We protect self-image before truth. We mistake salience for importance. We use reasons to defend what we already wanted. We remember stories better than records. We seek scapegoats when systems become too complex to face.

That is the sober anthropology underneath this appendix.

The solution is not to hand civilization to machines. The solution is to give humans personally-owned fiduciary agents that help us cooperate beyond our unaided limits.

Humans should remain the source of values, consent, legitimacy, love, meaning, embodied experience, and democratic authority.

Digital twins should provide the cooperation scaffolding: memory, provenance, evidence review, negotiation, calibration, privacy protection, bounded authority, attention defense, and reciprocal trust.

In this sense, personally-owned digital twins are not merely assistants. They are cooperation exoskeletons.

They help humans do together what humans cannot reliably do alone.

And if they are personally owned, fiduciary, verifiable, and reciprocal, they may become the first social technology capable of letting human plurality scale without collapsing into manipulation, scapegoating, institutional capture, or tribal war.

That is why humans are poor cooperators, and personally-owned digital twins will be better.
